NVIDIA Rubin HPC Render
Adding to a busy SC26 conference, NVIDIA has announced that they are developing a new GPU that will be targeted specifically at high-performance computing workloads. Aptly named the Rubin HPC, the future chip will be an HPC optimized version of the company’s Rubin GPU architecture. It would mark NVIDIA’s first significant HPC-class part since the Hopper generation almost 4 years ago.
This week’s announcement comes amidst a broader degree of soul searching that has been taking place over the part couple of years about the future of classic HPC workloads and the hardware that will run them. With commercial GPU server demand shifting over to AI-related tasks and low precision math over the last half-decade, server GPU designs have been favoring large arrays of tensor cores and other design choices that play better to AI needs. This has left traditional science and engineering users with fewer options than they have previously enjoyed, as the bulk of the prior decade saw server GPU designs treat HPC as a first-class citizen, if not a top customer.
Consequently, NVIDIA’s announcement of a dedicated HPC chip is a significant one. After the company all but sat out the HPC market with its Blackwell generation of parts, there was a question whether the leader of the AI revolution would even bother with the smaller HPC market. The answer to that turns out to be an unambiguous “yes,” though not until 2028 when the Rubin HPC chip is released. Nonetheless, it is a clear signal that NVIDIA does not intend to permanently secede the HPC (or supercomputer) market to rivals like AMD and Intel, who have been splitting up the market in recent years.
Rubin HPC: 50K+ CUDA Cores, Coming In 2028
With NVIDIA’s Rubin HPC chip not slated to arrive until 2028, this week’s announcement from the company (and a very visible VP of Hyperscale and HPC, Ian Buck) is in effect a teaser with more details to come. The company only had a few key details to share about the chip for this week’s announcement.
NVIDIA SC26 Rubin HPC Summary
The headline news here is that NVIDIA’s future HPC chip will over more than 50,000 CUDA cores – NVIDIA’s ALU arrays for classic vector/SIMD processing. This is around twice as many CUDA cores as NVIDIA’s current flagship Rubin SoC, and it is of great importance to the HPC market as few HPC workloads can make heavy use of matrix multiplication and NVIDIA’s tensor cores. An ideal HPC processor needs to be a great vector processing machine and not (just) a tensor processing machine, so the announcement of a large number of CUDA cores underscores just what kind of GPU this will be.
Painting broader strokes about the design of the rest of the GPU at this time, NVIDIA is not sharing any more details about expected performance or the memory subsystem for the HPC chip. Instead, the company is touting a “balanced design” that emphasizes growing compute and data movement capabilities together, rather than jump ramping up compute throughput on its own.
NVIDIA SC26 Rubin HPC CUDA Cores
This is (presumably) a reference to the chip’s other marquee feature, which is NVLink 7 support. NVIDIA’s current Rubin server GPU is on NVLink 6; in fact, it is the first chip to offer it. Which means that Rubin HPC’s scale-up networking technology will be a generation beyond that when it launches in 2028.
Reading between the lines a bit, the high-level specifications for Rubin HPC seem to be more closely tied to NVIDIA’s mid-generation refresh part for the Rubin lineup, Rubin Ultra . With it not set to be available for another year, there is only a paucity of information available on that chip as well, but most notably we already know that it is going to be the first chip to ship with NVLink 7 support. Which lends credit to the idea that the 2028 Rubin HPC chip following it will be closer to a Rubin Ultra derivative than it will be of the original Rubin server chip.
Rubin Ultra NVL576
That 2028 timeframe also lines up with giving Rubin HPC access to newer HBM4e memory, rather than the HBM4 used on the current Rubin server chip.
Past that, NVIDIA has also included a render of the chip in their SC26 presentation as well as on their newsroom article, which showcases a chip that looks very similar to their current Rubin GPU renders. NVIDIA chip renders are often more aspirational or illustrative than technical this far out, but if it is at least physically accurate then we are looking at 8 stacks of HBM spread out across multiple dies, the same as the current Rubin server chip.
Finally, for this week’s announcement NVIDIA has very briefly touted what they are calling a “sparse data acceleration” capability to keep the GPU cores fed, though with no other details on how this might work. The company’s tensor cores have long supported sparse matrices, though this would seem to be something beyond that, especially with the emphasis on vector math and CUDA cores.
NVIDIA HPC Accelerator Specification Comparison

CUDA Cores | >50000 | 18944 | 16896
Tensor Cores | Fewer? | 592 | 528
Memory Clock | HBM4E? | 8Gbps HBM3E | 6.4Gbps HBM3
Memory Bus Width | 2x 8192-bit? | 2x 4096-bit | 6144-bit
Memory Bandwidth | TBD | 8TB/sec | 4.8TB/sec
VRAM | TBD | 192GB | 141GB
FP32 Vector | TBD | 75 TFLOPS | 67 TFLOPS
FP64 Vector | A Whole Lot | 37 TFLOPS | 34 TFLOPS
FP64 Tensor | TBD | 37 TFLOPS | 67 TFLOPS
INT8/FP8 Tensor | TBD | 9 P(FL)OPS | 3.96 P(FL)OPS
Interconnect | NVLink 7 | NVLink 5 18 Links (1800GB/sec) | NVLink 4 18 Links (900GB/sec)
GPU | Rubin HPC | B200 | GH100
Transistor Count | ? | 208B (2x104B) | 80B
Manufacturing Process | TSMC 3nm? | TSMC 4NP | TSMC 4N
Architecture | Rubin | Blackwell | Hopper
In lieu of specific performance figures, NVIDIA is at least emphasizing that Rubin HPC will be applicable to a wide range of precisions, from NVFP4 all the way up to FP64. While FP64 (and to a lesser extent, FP32) are the biggest focuses for classic HPC workloads, more recent software efforts have looked at lower precision math as well, if only to account for how GPU hardware has changed over the years. While it was always extremely unlikely that NVIDIA would remove low precision math format support entirely, if only for binary compatibility reasons, the emphasis on supporting the full range of precisions implies that we should not expect to see NVIDIA too heavily compromise them, either.
Still, the top line figure to watch here is going to be FP64 performance, both for vector and tensor operations. NVIDIA has essentially plateaued at a bit under 40 TFLOPS for FP64 since Hopper (with Blackwell Ultra being especially poor here at less than 2 TFLOPS), so a fresh chip with a much larger number of CUDA cores would give NVIDIA the means to significantly ramp up their FP64 performance, depending in large part on just how many FP64 CUDA cores they bake into the architecture. And for that matter, how much die space they take away from tensor cores to free up the space for that FP64 hardware.
Final Words
Wrapping things up, the announcement of their Rubin HPC GPU means that NVIDIA is going to be firmly putting its hat back into the ring for HPC after something of an absence over the last few years. With the company so heavily focused on AI performance with the Blackwell generation, the Rubin generation marks a chance to reset their position in the market, not to mention to take advantage of the technologies they have developed for it. NVIDIA will not be without competition, however, as AMD is going to be launching their HPC-focused Instinct MI430X accelerator in 2027, and Intel is preparing their PCIe-based GPU D-Series . Which means that for NVIDIA, they will have a fight on their hands if they want to retake a large portion of the HPC market or its close cousin, the classic supercomputer market.

source_document.body:
Maersk and Hapag-Lloyd announced today that their Gemini Cooperation’s AE1, AE2 and AE3 services will return to the trans-Suez route and Red Sea , replacing diverted voyages around Africa.
The changes, in a phased transition extending from December into January, affect Asia-Europe services, but their potential to free vessel capacity gives U.S. importers a reason to watch the rollout.
“They will now sail via the trans-Suez route instead of transiting via the Cape of Good Hope,” Maersk (OTC: AMKBY ) said in a customer advisory.
The shift marks another step toward restoring shorter shipping routes between Asia and Europe. It could also change how much vessel capacity carriers need to maintain those services, with possible consequences for capacity deployment elsewhere in their global networks. Those effects remain uncertain, however, as congestion and network adjustments continue to absorb shipping capacity.
Maersk, Hapag-Lloyd ( HLAG.DE ) and other global liners since late 2023 diverted scheduled services away from the Suez-Red Sea route after Yemen’s Houthi rebels attacked merchant shipping in support of Gaza. But ocean carriers are returning as Houthi attacks waned, and longer diversions increased costs and operating complexity.
Transition begins December 4
AE2 will be the first of the three services to make the scheduled transition, with the Mary Maersk, voyage 650W, starting its rotation at Ningbo on December 4. AE3 will follow with Alette Maersk, voyage 652W, starting at Shanghai on December 20. AE1’s first listed sailing will be Damietta Express, voyage 702W, starting at Shanghai on January 14, 2027. These are dates at the first loading ports, rather than dates for passage through the canal.
The revised rotations include Suez Canal transits in both directions. Maersk said the changes would improve transit times, while cautioning that implementation depends on continued stability in the Red Sea and ongoing monitoring of regional security conditions.
The announcement also completes a broader routing shift within Gemini. According to shipping analyst Linerlytica, the return of these three services will make Maersk and Hapag-Lloyd the first alliance to restore Suez routing across all of its Asia-Europe services, following earlier changes to other Gemini loops.
U.S. impact centers on capacity, not direct routing
For the U.S. market, the impact is indirect. Shorter voyages can release vessels from longer rotations, creating opportunities for carriers to rebalance capacity across their networks, Maersk said.
That does not mean U.S. importers should expect an immediate drop in ocean freight rates. DHL Global Forwarding said the return to Suez would release capacity previously absorbed by diversions around Africa, but warned that congestion and extensive network adjustments could keep supply chains under pressure into 2027. And, recent violent incidents involving shipping in a global swath from the Black Sea to the Strait of Hormuz to the Somali coast create a tenor of uncertainty further supporting higher ocean rates.
Congestion and security remain constraints
DHL estimated that broader network adjustments could take another six to 12 months as carriers reposition vessels and rebalance services, assuming security conditions do not force further changes. It also said more than 10% of the global container fleet remained tied up in port congestion.
For cargo owners, that means increased vessel availability and dependable delivery schedules may not arrive together. Maersk’s own security caveat also leaves open the possibility that the announced rotations could change if conditions in the Red Sea deteriorate.
Why it matters: For U.S. importers, retailers and manufacturers, Gemini’s Suez return could loosen global vessel supply and influence future carrier deployment decisions, but congestion, regional demand and security risks will determine how much of that benefit reaches U.S. trade lanes.

source_document.body:
More than half of companies surveyed expect artificial intelligence to make or carry out more than a quarter of their day-to-day warehouse decisions on its own by 2028. That’s the finding of a new report from the Intelligent Logistics Systems Lab at MIT’s Center for Transportation & Logistics and Mecalux.
What’s Related
Some of those decisions are already being handed to AI. In 51% of the agentic AI applications described in the study, the software could decide to move inventory without a person’s approval. In 42% of cases, it could correct data on its own. Companies gave agents less authority over customer commitments and financial decisions.
Ninety percent of surveyed companies expect to spend more on warehouse AI over the next two to three years, and 29% expect spending to rise by more than a quarter. The report draws on responses from 1,967 supply chain and warehousing professionals across 21 countries.
RELATED: How to Set Up Warehouse Automation Without the Big Price Tag
What companies let AI do
Generative AI can draft training materials or help plan a warehouse layout. Agentic AI can take an action, such as deciding where inventory should go. Among companies testing or using generative AI, 57% used it to create documentation or training materials, and 53% used it to design warehouse layouts or processes. Handling exceptions and managing inventory were the two most common jobs for AI agents.
Companies drew tighter lines around decisions that affect customers or spending. In 22% of the agentic AI applications studied, agents could make commitments to customers without approval. Just 12% could make financial decisions. The most common setup let agents work within company-set rules while employees monitored their actions and could step in.
Most gains are still being measured
Sixty-one percent of surveyed companies said they had rolled out generative AI at scale or fully integrated it into their warehouses. Fifty-six percent said the same about agentic AI. About three in four applications had been at their current stage of deployment for less than a year.
Respondents reported at least moderate improvement in 87% of the generative AI applications they described in detail and 81% of the agentic AI applications. The share of companies that measured and documented significant gains was smaller: 39% for generative AI and 36% for agentic AI. Where respondents could estimate the improvement, the typical gain on the main measure they tracked was about 20%.
Some projects had already been dropped. Forty percent of companies said they had abandoned at least one generative or agentic AI project in the past two years. Trouble connecting the software to existing systems, poor data quality, and disappointing returns were among the reasons companies gave.
Existing software is an issue
Forty percent of respondents named integration with older systems as the biggest obstacle to expanding generative AI use. More than half said better connections to warehouse management and enterprise resource planning systems would do the most to speed adoption. Those systems hold the inventory and order records that many warehouse AI tools need to work.
Companies with detailed AI rules that they actively enforced were about twice as likely to report significant, documented gains. The researchers found that link after accounting for factors such as budget and how far along a company was in rolling out the technology.
How warehouse jobs are changing
Fifty-six percent of companies said the main effect on staffing was that employees moved to work for companies they considered more valuable. Eleven percent reported fewer jobs , while 9% reported adding staff.
Nearly three-quarters said they were training warehouse-floor employees in new skills, and 61% said they were creating technical roles. Researchers recommended setting rules for what AI can do before expanding its use and tracking results over the first 12 to 24 months before deciding whether to expand or drop an application.

The iX5 is BMW’s first fully electric vehicle built in the US, promising an estimated up to 456 miles of range, ultra-fast charging speeds, and plenty of Neue Klasse tech.
BMW begins iX5 production, its first US-built EV
BMW officially opened its new Plant Woodruff in South Carolina on November 13, marking the start of series production of its sixth-generation (Gen6) electric vehicle batteries.
The Gen6 batteries will power BMW’s upcoming “X” electric vehicles, starting with the all-new iX5 SUV.
The iX5 is being built about 15 miles away at BMW Group Plant Spartanburg, the company’s first fully electric model to be assembled in the US.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
BMW Plant Spartanburg is churning out around 70 iX5s a day following a $1.7 billion investment in South Carolina to expand the plant for EV production and build the new battery assembly plant in Woodruff.
According to Robert Engelhorn, president and CEO of BMW Manufacturing in Spartanburg, the company is confident the iX5 will attract buyers, promising 435 miles of range, ultra-fast charging, and its updated Neue Klasse technology and design.
Opening Ceremony of BMW’s new EV battery plant in Woodruff, SC (Source: BMW)
Engelhorn told Automotive News in an interview that “there’s a clear trend globally for EVs,” adding that “We will contribute to this growth from the BMW side.”
BMW didn’t provide a specific production estimate for the iX5, but suppliers were reportedly told it would be around 60,000 EVs in 2027, down from 100,000 it initially forecasted.
“We said we would begin assembling fully electric BMW vehicles in the US by the end of 2026 – and we are delivering on that commitment,” Engelhorn said.
BMW iX5 60 xDrive M Sport Package (Source: BMW)
A company spokesperson confirmed that the iX5 will initially use battery cells from China before switching to US-sourced cells from LG Energy Solutions plant in Arizona by the end of the decade.
With production now underway, the iX5 is expected to begin arriving at US dealerships in early 2027.
The 2027 BMW iX5 60 xDrive starts at $79,800. BMW estimates the 144 kWh battery will provide up to 456 miles of range, up from the 435 miles it previously estimated.
BMW iX5 60 xDrive hits 460 kW (Source: BMW)
It features BMW’s new “double-X” light signature, which combines the headlights, daytime running lights, side lights, and turn signals into one unit. The Double-X headlights come standard, but BMW said you can switch them for simpler diagonal stripes.
Last month, BMW showcased the i5’s ultra-fast-charging capabilities during a media event in Southern California with IONNA and Alpitronic.
During the demo, the iX5 60 xDrive hit a peak of 464 kW, which BMW said enables it to add an impressive up to 170 miles of range in 10 minutes.
BMW iX5 60 xDrive interior with M Sport Package (Source: BMW)
The electric SUV features a dual-motor all-wheel-drive powertrain setup that delivers a combined 578 hp (425 kW) and 593 lb-ft of torque. BMW says it can go from 0 to 60 mph in 4.4 seconds and tow up to 6,000 lbs.
Inside, the iX5 adopts BMW’s Neue Klasse design and tech, like the smaller iX3 SUV. The setup includes a new 17.9″ infotainment touchscreen and BMW’s Panoramic Vision, which spans the bottom of the windshield. There’s also an optional 14.6″ passenger screen for a third display.
BMW iX5 60 xDrive interior with M Sport Package (Source: BMW)
Measuring 197.2″ long, 78.7″ wide, and 68.9″ tall, BMW’s new iX5 is about the size of the Porsche Cayenne Electric.
By 2030, BMW plans to be assembling at least fully electric models at Plant Spartanburg. “This marks the beginning of the next chapter in the success story of the largest plant in our global production network,” Raymond Wittman, BMW’s head of production, said.
Following Debrecen (Hungary), Irlbach-Straßkirchen (Germany), and Shenyang (China), Woodruff is the fourth site in BMW’s production network to begin series production of the Gen6 batteries.

Ocean bookings eased to the 43rd percentile from 48th, and the rejection rate edged down to 12.77%, moving to the 77th percentile from 78th. U.S. Army Vice Chief of Staff, Gen. Christopher LaNeve, speaks at the 2026 AUSA Annual Meeting and Exposition in Washington, D.C., Oct. 12, 2026. (U.S. Army photo by Staff Sgt. Alexander Nieves)
WASHINGTON — The White House has officially nominated Gen. Christopher LaNeve to be the Army’s Chief of Staff after several months of serving as both the vice chief and acting chief of the service, according to a recently posted Congressional notification .
President Donald Trump has also nominated Lt. Gen. Marcus Evan s to succeed LaNeve as t he service’s vice chief.
LaNeve has been acting as the Army’s to p uniformed leader since Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth ousted former Chief of Staff Gen. Randy George in April . LaNeve, a former 82nd Airborne Division commander, took over after then-Vice Chief Gen. James Mingus retired a full two years earlier than expected . Notably, LaNeve served as a military aide to Hegseth prior to his current role.
Though LaNeve has only served as chief in an acting capacity, he has already made considerable change s to the service. He’s issued ne w doctrine on how the Army prepares for conflict through his “ How the Army Fights ” guidance, created a new Program Acquisition Executive for autonomy, redesignated the service’s Futures and Concepts Command as the new Army Futures and Autonomous Systems Command and more.
LaNeve’s nomination also comes as the Republican-led Congress approaches its scheduled end in January, potentially complicating his path to confirmation if the process extends into the new Congress. That gives current lawmakers a strong incentive to confirm the LaNeve before January.
Meanwhile, Evans most recently served as the special assistant to the commanding general for US Army Pacific Command, according to his service bio page . Prior to that, he was commanding general of the 25th Infantry Division and served as chief of staff at US Special Operations Command. He also served in combat in both Afghanistan and Iraq.
The nominations come as the Army remains without permanently confirmed top uniform or civilian leadership. T hen-Secretary Dan Driscoll resigned in September, and Adam Telle is currently serving as acting secretary. The White House has yet to nominate an official successor to fill the role.

source_document.body:
The argument for artificial intelligence in air cargo is no longer the hard part. The data foundation is finally in place, the forecasting problem is well documented, and consultancies have put numbers on the prize. The harder question is how an airline actually gets from a slide deck to a better decision on tomorrow’s 9 a.m. departure.
SmartKargo’s answer arrived on October 26. The Cambridge, Massachusetts, cargo technology company released the first four applications in what it calls its AI Apps portfolio, each aimed at a single part of the cargo P&L. )
A layer, not a replacement
The biggest design choice is how the apps connect. SmartKargo runs through APIs on top of whatever cargo management system an airline already uses, whether it’s a commercial product or one built in-house. There’s no migration involved, and SmartKargo says the apps can go live in weeks rather than years.
That matters in an industry where replacing a core cargo system is a multi-year, high-risk program. Airlines can also start with a single app and add the others later; each is independent and priced on usage, transactions or assets rather than seats.
Air cargo generated $151 billion in revenue in 2025, according to IATA, yet many decisions still run on static rules, manual overrides and delayed reports. SmartKargo frames every app around one test: does it drive revenue, reduce cost or reduce risk? Chief Revenue Officer Olivier Houri put it bluntly, “At SmartKargo, we start with something far more useful than hype: a business question.”
Revenue: pricing that keeps pace with the booking curve
Cargo pricing has long been a weak spot. McKinsey & Company notes that more than half of a flight’s capacity is often booked in the final week, when yield volatility is at its widest. Static tariffs adjusted by hand are poorly suited to that window.
AIRCAM , the revenue and capacity management app within the SmartKargo platform, targets exactly that gap. It reads demand, capacity and market signals for each shipment and returns a rate recommendation inside the booking and quoting flow. It forecasts booked and unbooked demand, allocates belly and freighter space to the highest-value mix, and flags underpriced capacity.
Every recommendation shows its reasoning, a nod to revenue managers who will not accept a black box. And win-loss outcomes feed back into the model, so pricing improves continuously rather than at the next quarterly review. VietJet Cargo is the named early adopter.
Operations: from firefighting to forecasting
If pricing is where cargo makes money, operations are where it quietly loses it. A missed connection becomes a missed SLA, then an unhappy shipper. Most operations centers still learn about these problems after the fact.
AINOC, billed as an AI-powered cargo control tower, is designed to move that moment earlier. It draws on cargo milestones, flight and airport operations, weather and airspace data, and partner signals. Its models predict where a delay will occur and for how long, flag SLA risk, trace root causes, and rank every exception by business impact rather than by who is shouting loudest.
A generative AI layer turns that analysis into plain-language briefings for operations staff and executives. Notably, SmartKargo pitches the rollout cautiously: a typical pilot covers one hub and a couple of trade lanes before expanding across the network.
Assets and data: the unglamorous foundations
The two remaining apps tackle problems that rarely make headlines but quietly drain margin .
AIULD addresses unit load devices and ground equipment, where damage, loss and idle time are a chronic cost. It gives airlines one view across owned, leased and pooled assets, combining location and condition signals with utilization and loss-prevention models. Tracking runs on SmartKargo Eye, a flight-certified tracker that needs no fixed readers at each station.
AICTX may prove the most strategically important of the four. Air cargo still runs teletype-era Cargo-IMP, Cargo-XML, IATA ONE Record and customs filings side by side. AICTX translates between them in both directions, uses AI to catch missing or ambiguous data before it causes problems downstream, and lets partners connect without changing their own systems. Clean data is the input every other model depends on.
What to watch
Taken together, the four apps map neatly onto the industry’s three pressure points: revenue, operations and risk. The modular, no-migration approach lowers the barrier for carriers that have watched large system replacements run over budget and behind schedule.
The bigger shift is AI as an intelligence layer across the whole cargo operation: models that learn from every booking outcome, see disruption before it cascades, and clean the data the next model depends on. Because each app sharpens as it learns from an airline’s own network, carriers that start early stand to build an advantage that compounds.
For an industry that has spent years debating whether AI matters, that is the right shift in the conversation: from whether to how, and from promise to proof.

The Disko project in Greenland. Image: 80 Mile.
By: Staff Writer November 17, 2026
Greenland Energy (Nasdaq: GLND) agreed to acquire 80 Mile (LSE-A: 80M) on Nov. 12 in an all-share deal valued at about £74 million (US$98 million), bringing the partners’ Greenland oil exploration interests and 80 Mile’s mineral assets under one Nasdaq-listed group.
80 Mile shareholders would receive 0.0079485 Greenland Energy shares for each share held, implying a value of 1.28 pence. That represents a 28% premium to 80 Mile’s Nov. 11 closing price and a 71% premium to its Sept. 7 close, before the offer period began.
“This combination builds on our existing partnership and brings our respective Jameson Land interests under common ownership,” Greenland Energy CEO Robert Price said in the announcement. “It would simplify the development structure.”
The acquisition would broaden Greenland Energy’s portfolio beyond oil exploration into minerals and Italian biodiesel production. Its plans include a strategic review of 80 Mile’s Dundas ilmenite project within six months of completion, potentially leading to a farm-out or sale.
Greenland Energy shares were 2.5% stronger at US$2.04 Tuesday morning in New York, valuing the company at about US$89 million. In London, 80 Mile was 2.5% weaker at 0.858 pence.
Funding, permits
The fully diluted valuation was calculated using Greenland Energy’s Nov. 11 closing price of US$2.14 and an exchange rate of US$1.33 per pound. The value of the share consideration will fluctuate with Greenland Energy’s stock and exchange rates. Each company’s shareholders would own about half of the combined group.
Greenland Energy had US$22.7 million in cash and equivalents at Sept. 30, plus US$4.3 million in marketable equity securities, it disclosed in a Nov. 16 filing . Its cash balance was down from US$37.4 million at the end of June. The company raised about US$70 million before fees in April.
Greenland Energy has also agreed to provide 80 Mile with a £3-million unsecured convertible loan carrying 12% annual interest and a 12-month term. The funding is intended to bridge a cash shortfall: 80 Mile’s existing resources are insufficient to execute its strategy through completion, particularly the ramp-up of its Italian biodiesel operations, the companies said.
Disko-Nuussuaq
80 Mile’s minerals portfolio also includes Disko-Nuussuaq in West Greenland, which targets nickel, copper, cobalt and platinum group elements. Drilling began July 1 under a joint venture with USFM Corp., which agreed to fund US$30 million to earn up to 51%. Dundas is in northwest Greenland, while the group’s Italian assets include the Greenswitch biodiesel plant.
The partners’ Jameson Land Basin project is an onshore oil exploration venture in East Greenland. Greenland Energy has the right to earn up to 70% by funding the first two exploration wells.
The planned 2026 drilling program has been deferred, and the partners are targeting a permitting timeline in winter 2027. Greenland Energy said it is reviewing contractor commitments, equipment procurement and logistics to preserve cash during the delay.
The acquisition is expected to close in the first half of 2027, subject to shareholder and court approvals, Nasdaq approval for the new shares and applicable regulatory consents, including from Greenland’s government.

Ocean container freight rates remained elevated on major east-west trade lanes, even as container carriers’ growing return to the Red Sea and an expanding global fleet raised the prospect of downward pressure on prices in 2027.
Asia-Europe prices were broadly stable for the week ending Nov. 13, while trans-Pacific rates edged higher, according to analyst and SONAR data contributor Freightos (NASDAQ: CRGO ). Congestion, higher fuel costs and transportation disruptions continued to support prices, but carriers’ attempts to secure further increases faced resistance.
Container carriers are continuing to restore Asia-Europe services through the Suez Canal and Red Sea, reducing their reliance on diverted voyages around Africa. That’s been the case since late 2023, when Houthi rebels in Yemen attacked shipping in support of Gaza. At the same time, observers say recent violence involving merchant vessels in locations ranging from the Black Sea to the Strait of Hormuz and Somalia are likely helping to support higher rates, as well.
Maersk and Hapag-Lloyd announced on November 16 that their Gemini AE1, AE2 and AE3 services would return to the trans-Suez route, with the first departures under the revised arrangements scheduled for December and January. The changes remain dependent on continued stability in the region.
Shorter voyages reduce the time vessels spend completing service rotations, increasing effective shipping capacity. That shift coincides with substantial fleet growth, as Alphaliner figures put the containership orderbook at 15.12 million twenty-foot equivalent units, equivalent to 43.9% of the trading fleet, with fleet capacity projected to expand 9.2% in 2027.
Together, fleet expansion and shorter routes increase the risk that available capacity will outpace cargo demand, weakening carriers’ pricing power next year.
For now, lingering congestion and higher fuel costs continue to support Asia-Europe container prices, which the supplied market update places 40%–50% above year-earlier levels.
Asia-North Europe rates were broadly unchanged at about $3,400 per forty-foot equivalent unit, or FEU, although they were down 5% from the end of October. Asia-Mediterranean prices were also approximately steady at $4,300 per FEU.
The stability suggests that carriers’ early-November general rate increases failed to take hold, raising doubts about another round of mid-month hikes.
Carriers are responding to the demand lull by increasing blanked — delayed or cancelled — scheduled voyages to restrict available capacity. Published reports cite eight Asia-Europe sailings were scheduled to be blanked the following week, up from five.
French dockworkers and port staff were called to join a 24-hour stoppage on November 17, while Spanish terminals were recovering from a November 11 general strike whose impact varied by location. While centered in Europe, job actions and other disruptions have a nasty way of dominoeing through the supply chain.
Freightos noted that carriers are preparing further price increases for late November and December, with pre-Lunar New Year shipping demand potentially providing stronger support.
Trans-Pacific rates remained near peak levels, edging up last week to $8,460 per FEU to the U.S. West Coast and $9,850 per FEU to East Coast hubs.
Other benchmarks showed some softening. Drewry’s World Container Index recorded weekly declines on Shanghai-Los Angeles and Shanghai-New York services, while forwarders reported discounts below published rates, highlighting differences between market measures and individual bookings.
Delays from inland challenges
Beyond ocean pricing, inland transportation continues to pose challenges. Containers moving by rail through Los Angeles and Long Beach face delays, with record Asian import volumes and storm-related disruption on BNSF’s Southern Transcon network worsening Southern California rail dwell times.
A November 20 strike deadline at LA-Long Beach involving watchmen with International Longshore and Warehouse Union Local 26 poses an additional operational risk, though contract bargaining continues.
US-China talks complicate the trade outlook
President Donald Trump is scheduled to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping this week, ahead of the January 10 expiration of the interim US-China trade agreement.
Although further de-escalation remains possible, divisions within the administration and renewed technology restrictions have added uncertainty. The Wall Street Journal reported disagreements among Trump’s advisers over the direction of China policy ahead of the summit. It’s also uncertain how China will approach dealmaking with the specter of a Democratic congress set to take control in January.
Washington has also moved to restrict Chinese access to advanced American artificial intelligence chips through overseas computing infrastructure, adding another point of friction before the talks.
The outcome could influence shipping demand and the timing of cargo movements as businesses assess the durability of the trade agreement.
Panama Canal eases restrictions as water conditions improve
Improved rainfall has allowed the Panama Canal Authority to ease restrictions introduced after lower-than-normal precipitation over the summer.
In a November 9 advisory, the authority increased total daily booking capacity to 34 transit slots and restored the maximum authorized draft for vessels using the Neopanamax locks to 50 feet. It cited improved water conditions, favorable hydrological projections and water-saving measures.
El Niño remains a risk, although recent forecasts have reduced the probability of an exceptionally severe event. Bloomberg reported that the US Climate Prediction Center lowered the likelihood of the event exceeding the strength of the 1982–1983 season to roughly 60%, from 83%.
Freightos sees a lower risk of severe canal disruption through the first half of 2027 than had been feared over the summer, although renewed restrictions remain possible.
Why it matters: Shippers face a market in which high current prices coexist with growing expectations of excess capacity. But cancelled sailings, labor disruption and inland congestion may continue to undermine reliability.

By: Northern Miner Staff November 16, 2026
Canada’s push to accelerate mining development risks running ahead of its workforce, with too few people available to meet demand over the next decade, Canadian Institute of Mining, Metallurgy and Petroleum President John Rhind says.
Recruiting younger workers and providing affordable electricity remain key challenges even as governments streamline project approvals, Rhind told The Northern Miner ’s Devan Murugan in an interview this month in St. John’s, N.L. Power costs could be a particular obstacle to development in Newfoundland and Labrador, he said.
“I would say the will is there,” Rhind said. “The ability to deliver is not quite yet.”
The warning comes as artificial intelligence, data centres and electrification drive demand that Rhind expects to sustain the current commodity upswing. Preparing the workforce should be the industry’s priority heading into 2027, with only a year or two to get training and recruitment on track to meet the coming decade’s needs, he said.

GM and Electrify America simplify EV charging
Public EV charging is getting easier and faster, with more DC fast-charging ports available and services like Plug & Charge that streamline payment.
The technology lets you start a charging session by simply plugging in the vehicle. The session is then billed through a linked payment method, so you don’t even need to swipe a credit card or use an app.
Eligible GM electric vehicle drivers enrolled in Energy Pass can now use the service at compatible Electrify America chargers.

The capability is now available for Chevrolet, Cadillac, and GMC EVs with a native CCS port (pre-2027 model year). Newer models, with a native NACS port, will gain the capability in early 2027, GM said.
“We’re making it easier for drivers to start a charging session and get back on the road, with an experience that has fewer steps than swiping a credit card to get gas.” Wade Sheffer, vice president of GM Energy, said.
(Source: General Motors)
Based on GM’s internal testing, the energy begins to flow within about 45 seconds of plugging the vehicle into the charger.
The charge session is then billed through your preferred payment method with Energy Pass. You can view session details and receipts in the myChevrolet, myGMC, or myCadillac app.
(Source: GM)
During the rollout, GM said drivers will still be able to use Charge by App and other charging methods.
How to get set up
To get started:
First, you’ll need to enroll in GM’s Energy Pass in the myChevrolet, myGMC, or myCadillac app.

Tesla has unveiled Powercore, a solid-state medium-voltage transformer that also handles the inverter and breaker functions in a single unit. Tesla rates it at 7.4 MW (9 MVA) continuously at 34.5 kV, with grid-forming support up to 10 MVA of peak power.
It’s made in America and scheduled to start operating in 2027. That’s the same year Heron Power, the startup founded by Tesla’s former top engineer Drew Baglino, plans to start volume production of its own solid-state transformer, the Heron Link.
Update: Tesla has since released a full spec sheet for Powercore, including efficiency, warranty, and its data center plans. We’ve updated the article with the new details.
Tesla’s transformer plan finally gets a name
Tesla first said it would build its own transformers in September 2025, when it unveiled Megapack 3 and Megablock . Megablock connects four Megapack 3 units to a transformer and switchgear, but Tesla shared next to nothing about the transformer itself.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
Powercore is that missing piece. Tesla announced it today through its Tesla Megapack account on X:
Introducing Powercore Solid state medium voltage transformer, inverter and breaker – reliable, safe and secure 7.4 MW/9 MVA continuously at 34.5 kVac w/ grid-forming support for 10MVA of peak power Made in America. Operating 2027 pic.twitter.com/sHxqnpWJrf — Tesla Megapack (@Tesla_Megapack) November 17, 2026
About an hour later, Tesla followed up with a much longer post on X laying out the full spec sheet:
Power: up to 9 MVA (7.4 MW) continuously at 34.5 kV AC
Peak power: 10 MVA for grid-forming
AC range: 10 kV to 34.5 kV
DC range: 800 V to 2,000 V
Peak efficiency: 98.86%
Availability: system guarantees of 99.9% and up
Warranty: up to 25 years
Operating range: -40°C to 55°C
It also packs a built-in solid-state medium-voltage breaker that Tesla says clears faults up to 1,000x faster than a conventional breaker. There’s no flammable oil, and it’s modular, so components can be serviced in the field without swapping the whole unit.
Tesla is pitching one product for three markets: battery storage, utility-scale solar, and 800 Vdc data centers. For Megablock, Powercore replaces the current two-step setup, where Megapack’s inverters output 480 V AC before a separate transformer steps it up to medium voltage. Tesla says that old architecture had twice the losses. For solar, Powercore works as a central inverter for today’s 1,500 Vdc arrays and upcoming 2,000 Vdc systems.
Tesla still hasn’t shared pricing, customers, or a factory location. It only says Powercore will be made in the US “of U.S. and imported parts” with first units operating in 2027.
The idea behind a solid-state transformer is simple enough. A typical solar or battery project uses low-voltage inverters to convert DC into AC, then a big oil-filled, iron-core transformer to step that up to grid voltage. A solid-state unit does both jobs with silicon carbide power electronics, which means less gear, a smaller footprint, and active control over voltage and frequency. That control is what “grid-forming” means: the unit can help hold the grid steady instead of just following it.
And with lead times on conventional transformers stretching into years as data centers and renewable projects pile into interconnection queues, there’s real demand for an alternative.
Heron had a head start
You can’t look at Powercore without thinking of Heron Power.
Baglino spent 18 years at Tesla and finished as SVP of powertrain and energy, in charge of batteries, motors, power electronics, and energy products. He left in April 2024 and launched Heron Power in 2025 to build solid-state transformers.
He brought a lot of Tesla’s power electronics talent with him. As we reported when Tesla first announced its transformer plans , Heron hired engineers who led power electronics design for Powerwall 3, the next-gen Megapack, and Superchargers, along with the person who ran Tesla’s power electronics controls team for charging and energy products.
Since then, Heron has raised a $38 million Series A, a $140 million Series B led by Andreessen Horowitz and Breakthrough Energy Ventures, and a $60 million credit facility from J.P. Morgan and TriplePoint Capital. Former Tesla CFO Zach Kirkhorn sits on its board, and Tesla co-founder JB Straubel is an investor.
It’s also building Heron Factory One, a 286,000-square-foot plant in Morgan Hill, California, designed to make 10,000 Heron Links a year. That’s over 40 GW of annual capacity, with commercial production planned for late 2027.
And the customers are lining up. Vantage reserved more than 1 GW for its data centers, Intersect reserved 1.5 GW, LG Energy Solution Vertech is integrating Heron Link with its US-made battery systems, and RWE signed a pilot to install Heron Links at a Texas battery storage site in April 2027. Baglino says Heron has 50 GW of orders in the pipeline.
Powercore vs. Heron Link
Here’s how the two compare based on what each company has disclosed:
 | Tesla Powercore | Heron Link
Functions | MV transformer, inverter, breaker | Replaces LV inverter and MV transformer
Continuous rating | 7.4 MW / 9 MVA | ~5 MW (solar/storage), ~4.2 MW (data center)
Peak | 10 MVA (grid-forming) | Not disclosed
AC voltage | 10 kV to 34.5 kV | Up to 34.5 kV
DC voltage | 800 V to 2,000 V | 600 V to 800 V
Grid-forming | Yes | Yes
Efficiency | 98.86% peak | 98.6% DC-to-MV; over 98.5% MV-to-800 VDC
Availability | 99.9%+ system guarantee; up to 99.7% per unit (data centers) | 99.5% lifetime availability
Warranty | Up to 25 years | Not disclosed
Data centers | MV straight to 800 Vdc, working with Nvidia | 34.5 kV AC to 800 VDC with integrated storage
Manufacturing | US, factory not disclosed | Morgan Hill, CA, 40 GW/year planned
Timeline | First units operating 2027 | Pilot April 2027, volume late 2027
Announced customers | None | Vantage, Intersect, RWE, LG ES Vertech
On paper, Powercore is the bigger box, and now it has the better numbers too. At 7.4 MW continuous, it carries about 50% more power per unit than the 5 MW Heron Link, and its 98.86% peak efficiency edges out Heron’s 98.6%. But Tesla’s figure is a peak number, and Heron doesn’t label its own as one, so it’s not quite apples to apples. Neither company has shared pricing.
Tesla is also going straight at Heron’s data center pitch. Powercore converts medium voltage directly to 800 Vdc, the rack architecture Nvidia is pushing, and Tesla says it’s working with Nvidia on 800 Vdc designs. Heron’s data center version does the same 34.5 kV AC to 800 VDC conversion with built-in storage, and data centers make up about a third of its business. Tesla’s answer to the storage piece is Megapack on the DC bus, and it says it already has 10 GWh of Megapack running at data centers.
Electrek’s Take
This one is a little awkward for Tesla.
A big chunk of the people who designed Tesla’s power electronics over the last decade now work at Heron, and the guy who ran the whole org is its CEO. Tesla’s energy business also lost its longtime leader, Mike Snyder, last month, according to the WSJ.
To be fair, Tesla still has plenty of power electronics expertise. Its silicon carbide inverters are in millions of cars and every Megapack. And it has something Heron doesn’t: a massive installed base and a sales channel. Tesla says it’s almost sold out of Megapacks for 2027, and bundling Powercore into Megablock is an easy upsell. Plenty of developers will take the one-stop shop.
Tesla’s specs now match or beat Heron’s on paper. But Heron has named customers, a pilot site with an install date, and a factory under construction. Tesla has none of those yet. I wouldn’t be surprised if Heron is actually ahead here.
But either way, the transformer shortage is big enough for both companies to sell everything they can build.

Oil prices are in the middle of their biggest downturn since the military action by the U.S. and Israel began at the start of March, and the benchmark price used for most fuel surcharges is trying to keep up.
The Department of Energy/Energy Information Administration average retail diesel price fell 19 cents/gallon effective Monday, published Tuesday, to $5.937/gallon. The one-week drop is the largest since a slide of 22.7 cts/g on June 22, and is the third-largest in the up-and-down (mostly up) movement in the volatile diesel market since the start of military action.
It’s also the first time the price has been less than $6/g since September 8. With the decline, the price is now down 59.2 cts/g since it set its all time-high of $6.529/g on September 22.
The DOE/EIA price is now several cents less than the AAA average daily price for retail diesel. That figure price dropped below the $6 level Monday, and on Tuesday stood at $5.9848/g.
And for the first time since September 10, the nationwide AAA average price for #diesel is less than $6/g. pic.twitter.com/LClDwWuYbp — John Kingston (@JohnHKingston) November 16, 2026
The latest DOE/EIA decline follows a rapid drop in the petroleum “complex” in the last several trading days in trading on the CME commodity exchange. Given the lag in retail pricing, barring a reversal, there are more declines to come at the pump.
Ultra low sulfur diesel (ULSD) settled at $4.4216/g on November 2, the first trading day of the month. After an enormous selloff Monday when ULSD settled down 20.47 cts/g at $4.0818/g, the price is down about 34 cts/g in the first half of November.
The decline in diesel futures prices have tracked the slide in crude, with the already enormous margin between diesel and crude –high by historical standards–holding steady on both the comparison between global crude benchmark Brent and first-month ULSD as well as second-month ULSD.
Brent settled at $104.77/barrel on the first trading day of the month. It settled Monday at $92.44/b and hit its October low settlement on October 10 at $91.49/b.
Where is the push coming from?
With most analysts having predicted continued higher prices, the question is what is driving the decline?
The market’s bears got a big boost last week with the release of the November supply/demand report from the International Energy Agency.
The IEA report repeated something it was writing a year ago at this time: there will be lots of crude in the market.
That was the forecast going into 2026, but the ability of that prediction to come true was derailed by war in the Middle East.
However, the IEA is back for 2027. “After a decline of 4.8 million b/d in 2026, oil supply is expected to rebound by 6.6 million b/d, reaching an average of 108.1 mb/d in 2027,” the IEA wrote.
Already, crude supplies are rising, according to the IEA. It said September global supplies increased 3 million b/d and then added 2.3 million b/d in October to 105.4 million b/d. Meanwhile, the IEA sees global demand this year averaging about 104.3 million b/d, far less than supply.
But that surplus is going to be needed to replenish inventories, which the IEA said globally have fallen about 460 million barrels since the beginning of the war.
The rising supplies are as a result of increased flows–mostly of crude, with refined products still restrained–going through the Strait of Hormuz.
Can’t count on Hormuz stability
Amrita Sen, the director of market intelligence at the research firm of Energy Aspects, told CNBC in an interview that her firm’s estimate is that flows out of the Middle East through all routes are up to about 16 to 17 million b/d, compared to a pre-war norm of about 20 million b/d.
But to show the precarious nature of that supply, Sen also said loadings “have started to come off in the last week.”
The most bullish voice in the market for months has been that of Jeffrey Currie, the CEO of Real Macro and the former head of commodities research at Goldman Sachs.
Also in an interview on CNBC, Currie said the Strait is in a position whether “we don’t know if it’s open or closed.”
But there are strong flows emerging now, “and that caps the prompt barrels, but it doesn’t make the next one any cheaper. So you’re kind of stuck in this limbo land at about $95 (per barrel for crude).”
The uncertainty means that the market lacks “any ability to escape to the upside or any ability to really drop much lower,” Currie said.
Without a long-term resolution of the situation in the Strait of Hormuz, Currie said, “it’s very unclear how we’re going to get a resolution here.”

After securing $2.1 billion this May, AI-driven drug designer Isomorphic Labs is back with more money—a lot more—securing the industry’s largest private fundraise ever.
Isomorphic Labs has clinched a whopping $5 billion in series C funding, more than doubling its own $2.1 billion series B from May and breaking the industry’s record for most money raised in a single round.
The $5 billion series C was co-led by California investors Greenoaks and Sequoia Capital, with continued investment from parent company Alphabet, according to a Tuesday release . Altos Labs, another AI-focused drug discovery engine, previously held the title for biggest fundraise after its $3 billion debut in 2022.
For Isomorphic, the fresh $5 billion will fuel efforts to scale the biotech’s drug design engine, which combines “a suite of foundational simulation AI models that natively work across multiple therapeutic areas and drug modalities,” according to the company.
The cash will also support Isomorphic’s preclinical pipeline as the biotech gears up to enter the clinic. Isomorphic has yet to publicly disclose any assets but said it has produced preclinical results for internal programs in both oncology and immunology.
Venture capital
AI-fueled Isomorphic bags $2.1B, the second largest biotech round ever
Isomorphic Labs, which hasn’t yet disclosed a molecule or reached the clinic, breaks the recent trend of investors putting their money behind more mature and de-risked assets.
May 13, 2026
·
2 min read
·
Tristan Manalac
Read more
Isomorphic is also focused on building out an ecosystem of partners and global infrastructure “required to power the future of AI-led bioengineering.” So far, the Alphabet company has announced research partnerships with several Big Pharmas, including Novartis, Eli Lilly and Johnson & Johnson .
“Our drug design engine is generating molecules with unprecedented precision and speed,” Demis Hassabis, Isomorphic’s founder and CEO, said in a prepared statement. The 2024 Nobel Laureate winner is also the co-founder of Google DeepMind and chief scientist for Alphabet.
“This round enables us to accelerate our progress: building foundational biology models, deepening our systemic disease understanding, and driving our first therapeutic programs towards clinical trials to deliver tangible impact for patients,” Hassabis said.
The biotech intends to “unlock some of the hardest problems in drug discovery,” according to Isomorphic President Max Jaderberg.
London-based Isomorphic launched in 2021 and shared news of its first fundraise of $600 million in March 2025. To date, the company has raised at least $7.7 billion—all without ever disclosing a clinical program.

Rep. Virginia Foxx. Photo: USDA
An 83 year old Congressional representative who sent an embarrassing letter to a well-meaning 10 year old constituent on the topic of electric cars and climate change, where she seems to brag about saddling his generation with debt through a recent climate rollback she voted for, is currently losing her seat
Update: This article was originally posted on May 14, but we wanted to update it with news of the election result. As of now, with 100% of votes counted, Foxx is losing by 362 votes, but has requested a recount. We’re updating this article with the most current information on the race below.
Christian Mango is ten years old, and was encouraged by his elementary school class to write a letter about a topic of his choice, and mail it to a decisionmaker. Christian chose his Congressional representative, 83 year old Virginia Foxx.
Foxx is an 11-term Congresswoman in North Carolina, one of the most gerrymandered states in the nation , and was expected to win a 12th term in the heavily republican district, having previously proudly touted an endorsement from an enemy of the US who tried to overthrow the government . Her opponent is Democrat Chuck Hubbard , a former journalist and native of the district.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
10 year old suggests EVs, climate action
For the topic of his letter, Christian chose electric cars – which is what makes this story relevant to us here at Electrek . Christian laid out several points about EVs, stating that “they’re better than normal cars. They’re better for the environment. They pay less. And there’s no gas.” (All true! well done Christian).
Christian suggested that electric cars could be incentivized with a $5,000 tax rebate – lower than the $7.5k EVs used to get , but better than the $0 they get federally today (compare to the ~$20k in ignored costs that gas cars still benefit from ).
Christian went on to suggest action on climate change, stating “maybe there is still a chance for 6.5 million people to not die anymore and for the weather to get better just maybe glaciers stop melting.” Christian was probably referring to the number of people who die from air pollution globally each year (though several estimates suggest that number is actually higher , and Christian did conflate climate and weather… but we’ll give him a pass on this one, his heart is in the right place).
Christian was proud of his letter, as was his mother, Emily Mango, who said “he researched, cited facts, and made good arguments in his essay – an essay that had nothing to do with politics. He was proud of his essay.”
Congresswoman’s response sparks outrage from mother
But then he got a response, and that’s when things took a turn for the worse. Christian’s mother Emily angrily shared the response on Instagram , where it gained traction.
View this post on Instagram
Emily said Foxx’s screed was “disrespectful, hostile and unkind” and called it “demoralizing and reprehensible.” She said she had to speak to her son and teach him that this response was “not okay,” and that “nobody should talk to a child like that and nobody should talk to a teacher like that.”
I’d also add that it’s full of disinformation, and that it even seems to brag about the massive debt that Foxx has imposed on Christian’s generation.
Foxx’s response filled with climate/EV disinformation
Foxx includes six links, all from propaganda publications that deny the science of climate change. 3 are from from WSJ (2 of which are opinion pieces) and 1 is from Fox, both of which are owned by the same climate denier, Rupert Murdoch. 1 is from Washington Times, a tabloid founded by a religious cult (yes, really), and 1 is from another right-wing climate denying publication, National Review.
Notably, none of the six links have anything to do with electric cars.
In the text of the response, Foxx touts republicans’ “all of the above” energy policy, which is ironic given that the party whose energy policy she touts has spent most of the last year forcing broken dirty coal plants open (which they are still doing after ruled illegal ) and trying to shut down clean cheap ones . Apparently “all of the above” is code for “fossil fuels and nothing else.”
Foxx’s letter does not directly address the strengths of electric cars, despite them being the subject of Christian’s letter. Notably, EVs actually can receive energy from any generation method, whether it be wind, solar, or even coal or gas – whereas gas-powered vehicles can only use one type of energy, oil. Thus, an “all of the above” strategy should probably find EVs the preferable route for transportation.
But in apparent contradiction to Foxx’s surely sincerely held belief that we should pursue an “all of the above” energy policy – which electric cars would help to achieve – she in fact has voted against EVs when given the opportunity.
Foxx voted against EVs, for giveaways to wealthy
Foxx claims in her response that she can’t support tax credits on electric cars, because those go to “mostly people with higher incomes who are able to purchase ‘new’ electric cars.”
But she in fact voted against, and later voted to repeal, incentives which were limited to lower-income-earners and were only available on cars up to a certain MSRP cap. Further, they were available on used vehicles, not just new ones – suggesting that Foxx doesn’t know what she voted against.
Foxx was one of 218 republicans to vote in favor of a ~$4 trillion giveaway to wealthy elites . Her vote raised electric bills and threatened US energy security and surrendered US manufacturing jobs to China . Some of the money given away to wealthy elites in the bill was clawed back from energy efficiency programs that had been going to regular Americans .
Those energy efficiency programs had been instituted by the Inflation Reduction Act, the Biden-era law which established tax credits for EVs and other efficiency rebates. The Inflation Reduction Act was actually revenue positive , which is to say it reduced the national debt ( by $238B ), rather than adding to it, because of provisions to increase enforcement against wealthy tax cheats.
But most of the IRA was repealed by the bill that Foxx voted for, meaning the US lost out on those deficit reductions. All in all, the bill Foxx voted for would add $4 trillion to the national debt – which, incidentally, is another point Foxx touches on in her response.
And she mocks a 10 year old over the trillions in debt she voted for
In one sentence, she seems to directly mock Christian, telling him that “YOU and your classmates will be responsible for that debt” as part of a warning about the dangers of government debt.
But I read this sentence as mockery, rather than as a sincere warning, given that Foxx voted to add $4 trillion to the national debt, which she, at 83 years old, knows she will not have to pay off. Christian, who is 10, will likely spend his whole life saddled with the debt Foxx voted for.
He will also have to pay for her inaction on climate change, which will have increasingly worse effects on the world Christian will grow up into. Foxx’s generation has already felt the heat, with the massive floods that devastated her state in 2024 , from a hurricane that was made 200x more likely due to climate change . Now, imagine how much worse it could get if Foxx’s policies remained in place until 72 years from now when Christian will be her age.
Foxx then closes out the letter with disparaging remarks about teachers, claiming that they are “too interested in indoctrinating you,” and warning Christian about “propaganda.” Which I guess shows where Foxx’s attitude comes from – if she has spent her 83 years never trusting anyone who knows more than her about a topic, that would certainly lead to the ignorance reflected in her letter.
Foxx – who somehow has a doctorate in education and currently sits on the Congressional education committee – could have turned this into a nice moment to teach the child who wrote her something about democracy and responsive government, but instead turned it into a moment to teach the world what’s wrong with her.
Update: Foxx may get her just deserts – she’s currently losing her seat by the narrowest of margins
When we first wrote this article, Foxx had a projected 97% chance of winning in a district which voted for her by a 19% margin in 2024 .
But that was before America (and its short memory) was reminded of how incapable republicans are of leading anything.
After a pile of economic crises caused by Donald Trump’s incompetent “leadership,” and his continued participation in an 8-month-and-counting war of choice that is spiking energy prices worldwide , bringing oil profits to record highs (and attempting to distract the news from talking about the Epstein files, which he is heavily featured in and has tried to cover up), America was once again fed up. And his incompetence took his entire party down with him.
Safe republican seats were flipped around the country in the biggest “wave” election we’ve seen in recent times, with the Democrats gaining control of both the House and Senate.
And it looks like Democrat Chuck Hubbard, a Wilkes county native and former journalist, who also ran against Foxx in 2024, will now get his chance to represent the people of North Carolina’s 5th district… assuming a recount goes in his favor.
The situation in North Carolina is particularly interesting, given that republicans had done an emergency redraw of district lines in an attempt to cheat their way to winning more seats .
Generally, district lines get redrawn after each Census, which happens on the decade mark, rather than mid-decade. But republicans saw ahead of time that they were likely to lose the House due to their unpopularity, and wanted to fudge the numbers in several states instead of going for a fair fight.
Top comment by James
Liked by 46 people
Foxx’s main argument against Christian’s suggested $5,000 EV incentive, is increasing national debt. Yet in just one tax bill, her approval increases the national debt over 10%. This is not Christian’s “responsibility”, this burden is forced on him, along with climate change.
View all comments
So they engaged in Gerrymandering , a process wherein district lines are redrawn to favor a particular political party. The idea is to put as many of your opponents’ votes into a few safe seats as possible, while spreading out your own votes to a wider range of seats that you win each by a small margin.
But it turns out that republicans were even more unpopular than they thought, and as a result, their Gerrymandering backfired . VIENNA — The leaders of the U.S., Russia and China are set to meet in the Chinese tech metropolis of Shenzhen on Thursday in an event that has been hailed as “historic” by all sides. Among the topics raised for discussion are reductions in global nuclear stockpiles. But experts caution that while the meeting itself is a positive development, any major breakthrough remains unlikely.
Expectations for the get-together ratcheted up over the course of the past week, particularly in Russia, where the event has been ascribed undertones of a “Yalta 2.0,” referencing the 1945 conference that reordered the world after World War II.
From the U.S. side, meanwhile, the Trump administration surprised many observers by pushing for discussions about reducing nuclear weapons while in Shenzhen. The last strategic arms control treaty between Russia and the U.S., in the form of New START, expired in February, leaving the two largest nuclear states without numerical limits on atomic arsenals for the first time since 1972.
China, meanwhile, was not a party to New START and was, in fact, never part of any strategic arms treaty like it. Beijing is estimated to have the third-largest nuclear arsenal in the world, at several hundred, although analysts believe it has been working to significantly increase this number in recent years. The U.S. and Russia each have stockpiles of around 4,000 nuclear weapons.
This numerical discrepancy is also why China has previously bristled at the idea of discussing strategic arms limitation in a trilateral format like the one U.S. President Donald Trump has been pushing in the run-up to the meeting. Although Beijing has confirmed the meeting, it has stopped short of officially saying strategic arms dialogue would be on the agenda. “The three presidents will have an in-depth exchange of views on safeguarding world peace and enabling strategic stability in major-country relations,” said Mao Ning, spokesperson for the Chinese Foreign Ministry.
This avoids naming explicitly what the U.S. has asked for. “The President has made it clear that, among other topics, he will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world. This proliferation, President Trump believes, is very dangerous,” White House spokesperson Olivia Wales told reporters last Friday.
Nikita Degtyarev, research coordinator at the Vienna-based Open Nuclear Network, an international NGO dealing with nuclear arms control, said he was realistic about achievable outcomes.
“I don’t have very high expectations, but I’m happy that it’s happening,” he said in an interview. “A meeting at the leader level is something else than the ongoing P5 dialogue and other existing formats.”
The P5 dialogue brings together the five Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty-recognized nuclear weapons states – the U.S., Russia, China, France and the U.K. – on a working level to discuss nuclear policy and risk reduction.
“If there is any outcome of the trilateral meeting relating to nuclear issues, it will likely be more of a political statement than a verifiable and restrictive arms control agreement,” said Heather Williams, director of the Project on Nuclear Issues and senior fellow at the Washington-based think tank CSIS ,
“I think the most likely significant outcome would be a reiteration of the Reagan-Gorbachev mantra that a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought,” Degtyarev said. A more substantive or groundbreaking agreement was also unlikely because there simply wasn’t enough time for lower-level officials to hammer out the details of any possible agreement that the leaders could sign, he said.
Major arms control treaties often take years of meticulous crafting at the working level before heads of state come together to sign them.
Trump first raised the topic of denuclearization in the context of the summit to reporters on Oct. 19, a day after the Wall Street Journal first reported about a proposed trilateral meeting.
A possible wildcard agenda item remains in the form of artificial intelligence in nuclear weapons. AI in nuclear command and control has emerged as a somewhat more promising topic and a potential area for agreement more palatable to all sides than commitments to numerical reductions or verification mechanisms.
The South China Morning Post reported Nov. 11, citing sources familiar with preparations, that working-level teams had discussed AI in critical weapons systems and that the agenda was shifting toward potential common ground, particularly AI’s role in nuclear command and control. One source characterized AI governance of nuclear weapons as an “easy deliverable” consistent with past policies.
This “could give Trump something to announce without requiring anyone to compromise their nuclear posture,” Lizzi Lee, a fellow at the Asia Society Policy Institute, told the French press agency AFP .
Under the previous U.S. administration, Biden and Xi reaffirmed the importance of human decision-making in nuclear command and control in November 2024, while Russia has so far resisted such language, including in the P5 process.
Much may depend on the willingness of Beijing to engage in strategic arms dialogue, which has indicated it has no major desire to discuss this topic while China remains a numerical underdog in the quantity of its warheads.
“China is the host and will probably closely stage-manage the event and the agenda,” Degtyarev said. Xi Jinping’s style of international engagements tends to be highly scripted and predictable, at odds with Trump’s more improvisational approach.
The common denominator for all three leaders is more likely to be good publicity. “Trump is probably genuine about his interest in nuclear arms reduction,” Degtyarev assessed, “but probably also from a self-serving and PR point of view.”
Though the meeting is historic in nature for its assembling of a triumvirate of the world’s most powerful men, “the Yalta 2.0 comparisons are overblown,” said Degtyarev. “The scale of the historical moment is simply different.”

Analysts are broadly confident that povetacicept will notch an approval in IgA nephropathy by the end of the month, setting up “the next wave” for Vertex Pharmaceuticals.
Vertex Pharmaceuticals is nearing a critical inflection point. The FDA is set to decide this month whether to approve the company’s investigational IgA nephropathy medicine—a product that, according to analysts, could herald the next chapter for the drugmaker and potentially open up market opportunities worth billions of dollars.
Founded in 1989, Vertex won its first FDA approval in 2011 for the hepatitis C drug Incivek—though this would prove to be a commercial disappointment as competitors moved in and the company pulled it off the shelves in 2014. Just a year after Incivek’s nod, however, the FDA greenlit Vertex’s Kalydeco as the first drug to treat the underlying cause of cystic fibrosis (CF). This approval—along with those for four other CF medicines—would put Vertex on the map and dramatically change the outcome for patients.
Now, investors are looking for “the next wave” of products from Vertex, eager to see the company open a new avenue of growth outside of its CF wheelhouse, Myles Minter, biotech equity research analyst at William Blair, told BioSpace. Povetacicept, the fusion protein therapeutic currently under regulatory review for IgA nephropathy (IgAN), could mark the start of that next wave. The FDA’s decision is expected on or before Nov. 30.
Currently, Vertex’s business is heavily reliant on its CF portfolio. The company posted $3.44 billion in revenue in the third quarter, of which $3.27 billion came from its CF products. The twice-daily oral drug Trikafta made $2.44 billion, while the newer-generation, once-daily pill Alyftrek brought in $706 million.
“Vertex is looking for the next key franchise beyond CF,” Evan Seigerman, managing director at BMO Capital Markets, told BioSpace , adding, “I think investors had hoped it that it was going to be with pain or sickle cell [disease].”
These indications have been underwhelming, however. Journavx, Vertex’s non-opioid pain medicine approved in January 2025, made $58 million in the third quarter. Meanwhile, the CRISPR-edited gene therapy Casgevy, indicated for sickle cell disease and beta-thalassemia, logged $99 million in Q3 sales.
Like Minter, Seigerman believes povetacicept could be Vertex’s next golden goose. “There’s a real path to a multibillion-dollar product in povetacicept,” he said. BMO is particularly bullish on povetacicept, with analysts saying in a May 4 note that an approval could herald an evolution of Vertex “that may be nothing short of iconic.”
Earnings
Vertex’s quiet Q1 is calm before potentially ‘iconic’ renal evolution
While some analysts may regard Vertex Pharmaceuticals’ first quarter results as “unremarkable,” BMO Capital Markets wrote on Monday, the second half of 2026 could be big for the biotech, with the potential approval of IgAN therapy povetacicept.
