Indeed, the drugmaker is also studying povetacicept in generalized myasthenia gravis (gMG) and primary membranous nephropathy (pMN), which Minter said indicates the asset’s a pipeline-in-a-product potential.
“I don’t know if it’s going to be quite the size of the cystic fibrosis [franchise], but it could be a meaningful revenue contributor over the next couple of years, adding diversity to their revenue base,” he said.
Kewalramani’s gambit
When Reshma Kewalramani took Vertex’s reins in 2020, she was filling the shoes left by her predecessor Jeffrey Leiden, who, from the start of his tenure in 2012, led the growth of Vertex’s CF portfolio and drove the company’s expansion into gene therapies.
Kewalramani, who had served as chief medical officer under Leiden, was tasked with charting the next chapter of Vertex’s growth. “Part of her mandate . . . was to build a growth trajectory that was not solely relaying on CF,” Minter said, adding that she went about this in two ways. The first was to look for innovative products internally, a search that resulted in Journavx.
Kewalramani also looked outward, seeking potential partners and acquisition targets for external innovation. This quest would eventually lead to Alpine Immune Sciences, which Vertex acquired in April 2024 for $4.9 billion . It was through this deal that Vertex gained the APRIL/BAFF dual antagonist povetacicept.
At the time, Alpine was the biggest deal in Vertex’s history, Minter said.
Deals
Vertex Buys Alpine for $4.9B to Bolster Autoimmune and Inflammatory Disease Pipeline
Vertex Pharmaceuticals on Wednesday announced it is acquiring clinical-stage immunotherapy company Alpine Immune Sciences for $4.9 billion in cash, the largest acquisition so far this year.
April 11, 2024
·
2 min read
·
Tristan Manalac
Read more
Vertex went for the takeover even when Alpine only had data from a handful of patients to support povetacicept’s use in IgAN. Mid-stage findings generated by the biotech, released alongside the acquisition announcement, showed a 64.1% reduction in urine protein-to-creatinine ratio (UPCR) at 36 weeks in six treated patients. In kidney diseases like IgAN, UPCR is used as an indicator of kidney function.
Alpine’s preclinical data also supported povetacicept’s proposed mechanism of action, demonstrating strong binding affinity against BAFF and APRIL—proteins that play key mediating roles in the production of abnormal IgA molecules, a hallmark of IgAN. Aside from IgAN, Alpine had also been advancing povetacicept for myasthenia gravis and systemic lupus erythematosus.
Pipeline-in-a-product potential
Following the Alpine acquisition, Vertex continued to build up povetacicept’s profile in IgAN. The company ran the Phase 3 RAINIER study, which enrolled more than 605 patients. In March, Vertex touted a 49.8% reduction in proteinuria at 36 weeks as compared with placebo. RAINIER’s primary endpoint, proteinuria—or excess protein the urine—is a key indicator of kidney damage and function in IgAN.
These data “look very strong,” Minter told BioSpace . The results are “in the range, if not slightly better than the currently approved therapies” such as Otsuka’s Voyxact and Vera Therapeutics’ Trutakna, he added.
IgA nephropathy
Vertex’s Nephropathy Asset Delivers ‘Strong’ Late-Stage Data, Clears Path to FDA
Vertex Pharmaceuticals has a rolling biologics license application with the FDA for povetacicept in IgA nephropathy. With new data from RAINIER, the biotech expects to complete its submission by the end of March.
March 10, 2026
·
2 min read
·
Tristan Manalac
Read more
Given this strong late-stage showing, “I’m very confident in povetacicept getting approved,” Minter said, noting that Vertex is seeking accelerated approval for the drug—a regulatory pathway that allows medicines to be cleared based on surrogate endpoints rather than direct proof of clinical improvements.
“You’re getting deep proteinuria reductions that would be predictive of stabilization of estimated glomerular filtration rate [a measure of kidney function], which would be grounds for accelerated approval by the FDA,” Minter noted.
And once povetacicept has secured that first nod, Vertex will have a smoother time expanding into future indications, he said. “It’s a much easier regulatory path once you get that first approval to come back and do it again.”
Vertex is expecting a Phase 2 readout for povetacicept in gMG in the first half of next year, and is running the Phase 3 OLYMPUS study for pMN in which enrollment and dosing are “well underway,” according to a third-quarter presentation earlier this month.
“This is a molecule in multiple multi-billion-dollar indications,” Minter said, adding that even if povetacicept never reaches the heights of Vertex’s CF franchise, the asset would still be “meaningful for the company.”
A safety asterisk
Despite povetacicept’s strong efficacy profile, there is a safety signal that has investors leery, Minter said. At Kidney Week, Vertex was peppered with questions about the risk of hypogammaglobulinemia—a side effect characterized by a steep drop in IgG levels that in turn increases the risk of severe infections, according to the analyst.
Nearly half (46%) of povetacicept-treated patients in RAINIER developed infections, as opposed to 40.5% of placebo comparators, according to Vertex’s presentation . The majority of these episodes were mild or moderate. Severe infections were rare and balanced between the study groups. Still, RAINIER had a protocol in place that required patients whose IgG levels dropped below a certain threshold to “go on a drug holiday,” Minter said. Vertex hasn’t disclosed how many patients needed to pause treatment because of low IgG concentrations.
BMO’s Seigerman similarly acknowledged povetacicept’s infection risk but wasn’t too concerned. “What’s important is that the infection risk [was] balanced” between the povetacicept and placebo arms,” he said. For Seigerman, that’s what instills confidence in the drug’s safety profile.
“There’s a good safety profile, and the efficacy is very strong,” he said of povetacicept, adding that the drug offers a more convenient monthly dosing schedule via an autoinjector. Other injectable therapies in this space are given weekly—like Trutakna —while oral options such as Novartis’ Fabhalta are taken twice daily.
Of course, a rejection for povetacicept is not impossible. Both Minter and Seigerman said there is the remote possibility of povetacicept being rebuffed due to reasons beyond efficacy and safety, such as manufacturing challenges or violations at an external production plant.
Again, Seigerman wasn’t too worried, as Vertex has told him there shouldn’t be any issues on the manufacturing front. “I’m very confident that they’ll get approval,” he said.

Freight broker RXO said Tuesday that even though truckload spot rates have cooled in the fourth quarter, the market is not entering deflationary territory.
RXO’s ( NYSE: RXO ) linehaul rate dataset, which excludes fuel surcharges, jumped 37.9% year over year in the third quarter, to “levels not seen since peak COVID-era shipping.” So far in the fourth quarter, rate growth has slowed to plus-26.2% y/y, which is “still significantly higher than 2025 heading into peak season.”
“In Q4, the overall demand picture remains muted against an uncertain economic backdrop, but sustained pressure on the supply side of the market (carriers) has created a tight environment for shippers — and peak season is fast approaching,” the company’s Curve Report stated.
SONAR: National Truckload Index (linehaul only – NTIL.USA) for 2026 (blue shaded area), 2025 (yellow line), 2024 (green line) and 2023 (pink line). The NTIL is based on an average of booked spot dry van loads from 250,000 lanes. The NTIL is a seven-day moving average of linehaul spot rates excluding fuel. Rates remain significantly higher on a y/y comparison in November. To learn more about SONAR, click here .
SONAR: Outbound Tender Rejection Index (OTRI.USA) for 2026 (blue shaded area), 2025 (yellow line), 2024 (green line) and 2023 (pink line). A proxy for truck capacity, the tender rejection index shows the number of loads being rejected by carriers. Current tender rejections show a tight truckload market.
Strict regulatory enforcement and years of weak carrier profitability have drawn down capacity , significantly tightening the market despite flat demand.
While cost pressures dominated the headlines during the third-quarter earnings season, fleets are logging large contractual rate gains after a multiyear downturn. Knight-Swift Transportation ( NYSE: KNX ) is now targeting “at least double-digit [rate] increases” in its new bid season , which began earlier this month.
Cass Information Systems ( NASDAQ: CASS ) said Monday that linehaul contract rates (ex-fuel) were up for a 22nd straight month in October, 9.9% higher y/y. The dataset averaged rate increases of 10% in the third quarter, following a plus-6% average in the second quarter.
“The combination of federal policy enforcement, increasing insurance premiums, record-high fuel, and high interest rates has both reduced the available labor pool while making the financial barriers to entry much higher,” the RXO report said. … “As long as freight demand remains muted, there won’t be extreme market volatility, but any incremental increase in shipments could result in a very difficult market for shippers.”
SONAR: Contract Rate Change Direction (CRCD.USA). The dataset measures the average percentage difference between new and former contract base rates. Recent contract renewals are averaging 12%.
RXO’s all-in cost-per-mile index, which includes fuel surcharges, stood at 160.1 in the third quarter (indexed to a 2015 baseline). This is the highest reading since the 2022 first quarter. Diesel fuel prices were up 48% y/y in the quarter, but the report said diesel didn’t account for all the rate increase.
“A substantially higher cost structure has moved the baseline up for carriers, regardless of fuel costs.”
Why it matters? Driven by tightening capacity and higher operating costs, these rate trends signal a shift in market power toward carriers seeking margin improvement. Shippers should respond by securing dependable capacity and guarding against routing guide deterioration.

El Teniente mine smelter. ( Image courtesy of: Codelco | Flickr. )
By: Staff Writer November 17, 2026
Chile’s copper production is forecast to fall below five million tonnes this year for the first time since 2003, as lower ore grades and operational disruptions curb output while expensive imported sulphuric acid squeezes leaching operations.
Output is expected to decline 8.4% to 4.935 million tonnes in 2026, a loss of about 453,000 tonnes from last year, the Chilean Copper Commission (Cochilco) projects in its latest forecast . It expects a 3% recovery to 5.084 million tonnes in 2027.
“Higher input costs, notably diesel and sulphuric acid, are placing upward pressure on costs,” Capstone Copper (TSX: CS; ASX: CSC) said in its July 30 results.
The world’s largest copper-producing nation faces pressure at both ends of the production chain. Ageing deposits require more ore to be processed for each tonne of metal, while reduced smelting activity limits domestic supplies of the acid used to recover copper through leaching.
Acid cuts
At Mantoverde, Capstone changed its mine plan to prioritize sulphide production and reduce leaching of ore that consumes large amounts of acid. The change cut expected acid requirements by about 200,000 tonnes, eliminating additional spot purchases for the remainder of 2026, the company said in July.
Capstone maintained its overall cost guidance at that time, citing a greater share of lower-cost sulphide production and higher byproduct credits. Its response illustrates why the impact of higher acid prices varies between operations.
Chile produced about 385,100 tonnes of copper in September, down 15% from a year earlier. Output during the first nine months declined 8.5% to 3.633 million tonnes, according to Cochilco’s monthly data.
September production fell 21% at Escondida, operated by BHP (ASX: BHP; NYSE: BHP) with Rio Tinto (LSE: RIO; NYSE: RIO) as a partner, and 27% at BHP’s wholly owned Spence mine. Output rose 17% at state-owned Codelco’s El Teniente and 7.1% at Los Pelambres, which is 60%-owned by Antofagasta (LSE: ANTO).
Lower grades, maintenance and weather disruptions have constrained output. El Teniente has also faced restrictions following its fatal 2025 rockburst, although its September production improved against the accident-affected period a year earlier.
Cochilco’s 2026 forecast would leave Chile about 900,000 tonnes below its 2018 peak of 5.832 million tonnes. The projected recovery next year would replace only about a third of this year’s decline.
Acid dependence
Chile imported a record 3.97 million tonnes of sulphuric acid in 2025, exceeding domestic production and supplying about half of national consumption. Domestic output fell 17% to 3.92 million tonnes, its lowest level since 2002, Cochilco said in its acid market study.
The closure of Ventanas, suspension of Paipote and shutdown of Potrerillos, alongside disruptions at El Teniente, reduced acid production. Chilean smelters operated at about 60% of capacity on average in 2025, according to Cochilco.
Smelters make sulphuric acid by capturing sulphur-bearing gases released during copper processing. The acid is used to dissolve copper from ore before solvent extraction and electrowinning recover the metal as cathodes.
China supplied 37% of Chile’s acid imports in 2025 before restricting exports from May 2026. Disruptions to sulphur shipments through the Strait of Hormuz also raised costs for acid producers overseas, increasing pressure on Chile’s imported supplies.
Chile sustained supplies by buying from alternative sources, including Peru, Bulgaria and South Korea, and adding India as a supplier. China authorized an exceptional shipment of about 32,000 tonnes to Chile in September, but Cochilco cautioned that this did not represent a general reopening of exports.
Contracts cushion costs
The spot price at Mejillones in northern Chile rose from about $190 per tonne in late February to $500 in late April. Many large miners had signed contracts for 2026 at $160–$175 before the disruption, limiting their exposure to the surge, according to Cochilco.
Using Chile’s 2023 average acid consumption intensity, GEM Mining Consulting calculated that the acid input cost rose from about 42¢ per lb. of copper produced through solvent extraction and electrowinning to 73¢, comparing the 2025 average import price with July 2026 prices. That is an illustrative 74% increase in the acid component, rather than in total production costs.
Actual exposure depends on ore characteristics and supply contracts. Acid consumption ranged from 0.78 to 22.4 tonnes per tonne of cathode across operations in 2023 , Cochilco found.
Copper produced through leaching, solvent extraction and electrowinning accounts for about 21% of national output. GEM estimates that output proportionally exposed to imported acid represents about 11% of Chilean copper production, including 4% exposed to Chinese supply. Its allocation model does not identify individual mines’ suppliers.
Cochilco projects acid consumption by copper mining will rise 15%, from 6.9 million tonnes in 2025 to about 7.9 million tonnes in 2027. If domestic acid production stays at its 2025 level, the gap against mining demand alone would reach about four million tonnes.
